## Luke 9:42–62 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 42 — The Demon's Last Assault and Jesus' Deliverance

- **Gill (Baptist/Calvinist, 1771):** The demon, knowing who Jesus was and that he was about to be dispossessed, resolved to do all the mischief he could while still in the boy — throwing him down and convulsing him terribly as one last act of malice. Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit for its cruelty, then healed the child and "delivered him again to his father" — a phrase emphasising the father's joy at receiving his son back whole.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-42.html (Gill's Exposition)

- **Barclay (1959):** The word for "dashed him down" (Greek *rēgnymi*) is the same used of a boxer dealing a knock-out blow or a wrestler throwing an opponent. The scene was pitiful. Yet Jesus dealt with it with calm mastery.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-42.html (Barclay's Daily Study Bible)

- **Guzik / Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** This was the last, desperate effort of the possessing demon to hold on to the boy and cast everyone into despair. Jesus was not intimidated. What was too hard for the disciples was not too hard for Jesus.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/

- **Matthew Henry (1706):** Christ can do for us what His disciples cannot. Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit when it raged most. Henry adds that when children are recovered from sickness, parents should "receive them as delivered to us again, receive them as life from the dead."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-42.html (Henry's Complete Commentary)

---

### vv. 43–45 — Astonishment, Then a Sober Warning

**v. 43:** "And they were all astonished at the greatness of God."

- **Guzik:** Jesus had just revealed His glory in two spectacular ways — the Transfiguration and casting out a difficult demon. The crowd was marvelling at the majesty of God displayed in Jesus' works.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/

**v. 44:** "Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men."

- **Guzik (citing Clarke):** "To other words, you may lend occasional attention — but to what concerns my sufferings and death you must ever listen. Let them constantly occupy a place in your most serious meditations and reflections." Jesus deliberately punctured the triumphant mood.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/

- **BibleHub (Ellicott):** Literally "Set these sayings in your ears." The English "sink down" is an adequate idiomatic rendering. The verb "is about to be delivered" signals imminence; the title "Son of Man" identifies Jesus with Daniel's promised ruler who receives everlasting dominion — yet here He announces betrayal and surrender.
  — https://biblehub.com/luke/9-44.htm

**v. 45:** "But they did not understand this statement. It was veiled from them so that they could not comprehend it, and they were afraid to ask Him about it."

- **BibleHub (theological note):** The perfect-passive participle *kekrymmenon* ("having been concealed") denotes a completed, continuing state; the agent is implicitly God. The purpose clause ("so that they might not perceive") shows an intentional divine act of obscuration. Revelation is not merely data offered; it is insight granted by God. Luke delays full understanding until the Spirit's outpouring (Acts 2; cf. John 16:13).
  — https://biblehub.com/q/Luke_9_45_s_impact_on_divine_revelation.htm

- **Carson (Reformed, via Monergism):** The most important reason the disciples could not grasp it is given in the next verse — they were thinking in terms of greatness. While Jesus talked about His impending death, they were arguing about which of them would be the greatest in the kingdom. They assumed He was speaking in "some subtle, symbol-laden, metaphorical fashion that finally escapes them."
  — https://www.monergism.com/jesus%E2%80%99s-resolve-head-toward-jerusalem

---

### vv. 46–48 — True Greatness and the Little Child

**v. 46:** "Then an argument started among the disciples as to which of them would be the greatest."

- **Bible.org (Bob Deffinbaugh):** The disciples may have feared asking Jesus about His death, but they were not reticent to ask about their own positions in the kingdom. Matthew tells us they disguised their ambition by asking, "Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?" rather than openly stating their self-interest.
  — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/32-secular-saints-luke-937-56 (from search excerpt)

- **Carson:** This is parallel to Matthew 20:20–28 where Zebedee's wife asks for James and John to sit at Jesus' right and left. The apostles were "not focusing on death at all, still less on destruction and persecution… They think they already fully understand what messiahship and kingship are about."
  — https://www.monergism.com/jesus%E2%80%99s-resolve-head-toward-jerusalem

**v. 47:** "But Jesus, knowing the thoughts of their hearts, had a little child stand beside Him."

- **Guzik:** Jesus might have answered "who is the greatest?" by pointing to Himself. Instead, He drew their attention to His nature by using a little child. Jesus understood not just their conversation but "the thought of their heart" — their motives and impulses.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/

- **Carson:** "Jesus, knowing their thoughts, took a little child and had him stand beside him." In the flow of the argument, Jesus is saying: they want to be close to Jesus because He is great and becoming greater. But Jesus asks, in effect, "I want to see how you welcome a child." Welcoming a child gains no social advantage — it is the opposite of scrambling up a bureaucratic ladder.
  — https://www.monergism.com/jesus%E2%80%99s-resolve-head-toward-jerusalem

**v. 48:** "Whoever welcomes this little child in My name welcomes Me … For whoever is the least among all of you, he is the greatest."

- **Guzik:** In that culture children were of little importance, were not threatening, unconcerned for social status, and not jaded by success and ambition. "The principle being established by Jesus was that in the kingdom of God there is a reversal of values involved. The last will be first; the least will be the greatest" (citing Pate).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/

- **BibleHub (Pulpit Commentary / Ellicott):** The better manuscripts give "the same *is* great" — the greatness is not thrown forward as a future compensation but thought of as actually attained in the midst of the seeming humiliation. Also notes that this saying has been the inspiration behind countless child-homes, schools, hospitals, and the Sunday school movement.
  — https://biblehub.com/luke/9-48.htm

- **Bible.org (Deffinbaugh):** If you measure significance of ministry by the significance of your audience, then ministering to a child seems insignificant. Jesus taught that it does not matter *to whom* you ministered because all ministry should be ministry to Christ and for Christ. To welcome a child is to welcome Him.
  — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/32-secular-saints-luke-937-56 (from search excerpt)

---

### vv. 49–50 — The Outsider Casting Out Demons

**v. 49:** "Master, we saw someone driving out demons in Your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not accompany us."

- **Gill (Baptist):** John's remark was prompted by Jesus' words "in My name" (v. 48). The Syriac and Persic versions read "because he followeth not *thee* with us" — the man did not join their company or follow Christ as they did.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-49.html

- **Guzik:** This must have been frustrating to the disciples because it showed that other followers of Jesus were able to cast out demons when they sometimes were not (v. 40). No wonder John wanted them to stop.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/

- **Ellicott (Anglican, 1905):** The link to the foregoing context lies in the words "in My name" (v. 48). John, "young, warm, but not sufficiently apprehending Christ's teaching," asks, "Were we wrong?" Jesus replies: "Ye were wrong."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-49.html

**v. 50:** "Do not stop him, for whoever is not against you is for you."

- **Ellicott:** Christ does not say the man *should* not have followed with them, but simply teaches how he was to be regarded though he did not — as a reverer of His name and a promoter of His cause. "Surely this condemns not only those horrible attempts by force to shut up all within one visible pale of discipleship, which have deluged Christendom with blood in Christ's name, but the same spirit in its milder form of proud ecclesiastic scowl upon all who 'after the form which they call a sect … do so worship the God of their fathers.'"
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-49.html

- **StudyLight (sermon note):** This statement ("whoever is not against you is for you") appears antithetical to Luke 11:23 ("he that is not with me is against me"). The key is the differing occasions: here, someone is doing good in Jesus' name though not part of the inner circle — that person is to be regarded as an ally, not an enemy. Luke 11:23 addresses those who are neutral in the face of Christ's claims. Both are true in their contexts.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-49.html

- **Carson:** "How pathetic is that! They not only want to climb up the ladder … but they also want to crush any party that might provide any competition in this religion business." The disciples do not even ask whether the other group is doing good or speaking truth.
  — https://www.monergism.com/jesus%E2%80%99s-resolve-head-toward-jerusalem

---

### vv. 51–56 — The Samaritan Rejection and James and John's Zeal

**v. 51:** "As the day of His ascension approached, Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem."

- **Carson (Reformed):** Luke 9:51 is the great turning-point of Luke's Gospel. From here until the Triumphal Entry, everything takes place "under the looming shadow of the impending cross." Luke structures his "travel narrative" so that Jesus is repeatedly said to be journeying toward Jerusalem: 13:22, 17:11, 18:31–33, 19:28.
  — https://www.monergism.com/jesus%E2%80%99s-resolve-head-toward-jerusalem

- **Calvin (Reformed, 1540):** By the expression "He steadfastly set His face," Luke shows that Christ, with death before His eyes, rose above the fear of it and went forward to meet it. But at the same time it "points out that he had a struggle, and that, having vanquished terror, he boldly presented himself to die." Christ was not devoid of feeling; He was affected by the cruel and bitter death He faced. His resolve was not stoic indifference but a deliberate overcoming of natural dread — "a remarkable proof of his unbounded love to us."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-53.html (Calvin's Commentary)

- **Matthew Henry:** Jesus looked *through* His sufferings to the glory that would follow — He viewed it as the time when He would be "received up" into glory. "All good Christians may frame to themselves the same notion of death, and may call it their being received up." He "went cheerfully and courageously thither, though he knew the things that should befall him there."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-53.html (cited from earlier search excerpt)

- **Constable (Dispensational):** Luke presented what were really three trips to Jerusalem as one. The ministry of Jesus during this journey took on new characteristics: primary attention to the disciples, many words of warning to the rich and complacent as well as to the Pharisees.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-53.html (Constable's Expository Notes)

**vv. 52–53:** Messengers sent ahead into a Samaritan village; the people refused to welcome Him because He was heading for Jerusalem.

- **Clarke (Methodist/Wesleyan, 1810):** The Samaritans saw He was going to Jerusalem to keep the feast (the Feast of Tabernacles, John 7:2) and, knowing Him to be a Jew, would afford nothing for His entertainment. "In religious matters, the Samaritans and Jews had no dealings" (cf. John 4:9). Clarke calls them "a kind of mongrel heathens; they feared Jehovah, and served other gods" (2 Kings 17:34).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-53.html (Clarke's Commentary)

- **Barnes (Presbyterian, 1832):** The Samaritans had probably hoped Jesus would decide the temple controversy (Jerusalem vs. Mount Gerizim) in their favour. When they saw He was going to Jerusalem — thereby deciding the question for the Jews — "they resolved to have nothing to do with him." Barnes draws the application: people often reject true religion from selfish regard to their own views, "as the Samaritans did the Son of God, and bring upon themselves swift destruction."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-53.html (Barnes' Notes)

- **Constable:** The Samaritans rejected Jesus not because He claimed to be Messiah but simply because He was a Jew heading to worship at Jerusalem (cf. John 4:20).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-53.html

**v. 54:** "Lord, do You want us to call down fire from heaven to consume them?"

- **Coffman (Restoration Movement):** "Boanerges, 'The Sons of Thunder,' would have punished without mercy this wretched village of the Samaritans; but Jesus rebuked the very thought of doing such a thing." The apostles apparently believed they had such power — and with Jesus' permission, they did. That permission, however, they did not have.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-53.html (Coffman's Commentaries)

- **Constable:** James and John may have been thinking that Jesus would react as Elijah had to his opponents (2 Kings 1:9–12). Their question suggests they saw strong similarities between Jesus' ministry and Elijah's (cf. v. 19). However, they were willing to *play Elijah's part* by calling down judgment; they were not asking Jesus to do so.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-53.html

- **Carson (Reformed):** "Jesus heads toward Jerusalem to be killed, but he forbids killing the Samaritans who do not welcome him." The disciples wanted to call down fire; Jesus rebuked them.
  — https://www.monergism.com/jesus%E2%80%99s-resolve-head-toward-jerusalem

**vv. 55–56:** "But Jesus turned and rebuked them. And He and His disciples went on to another village."

- **Coffman:** The additions found in some ancient manuscripts and now relegated to the margin ("Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man came not to destroy men's lives, but to save them") are "nevertheless true to the meaning of the context."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-53.html

- **Coffman:** "Isn't it wonderful that God does not retaliate against sinful men, repaying evil with evil? A village rejected the only begotten Son, but he only went on to another village." Also notes a principle of missionary endeavour: "If not received in one place, let him go to another."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-53.html

### vv. 57–62 — The Cost of Discipleship: Three Would-Be Followers

**vv. 57–58:** "I will follow You wherever You go" / "Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head."

- **Guzik:** With the miracles associated with Jesus' ministry, following Him might have seemed more glamorous than it really was. Jesus "perhaps received many spontaneous offers like this." He warns the enthusiastic volunteer that following Him means embracing His homelessness — even animals have more settled lodging than the Son of Man.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/

**vv. 59–60:** "Lord, first let me go and bury my father" / "Let the dead bury their own dead. You, however, go and proclaim the kingdom of God."

- **Guzik:** This man did not ask for permission to dig a grave for a deceased father. He wanted to remain in his father's house and care for him until the father died — "this was obviously an indefinite period, which could drag on and on." Jesus' reply is deliberately shocking: let the spiritually dead bury the physically dead. The urgency of proclaiming the kingdom takes precedence over even the most sacred family obligations.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/

**vv. 61–62:** "I will follow You, Lord; but first let me bid farewell to my family" / "No one who puts his hand to the plow and then looks back is fit for the kingdom of God."

- **Guzik:** The previous man offered a potentially long delay; this man asked for only a relatively short one. Yet both are rebuffed. The image of ploughing: a farmer kept rows straight by focusing on an object ahead in the distance. Looking back ruins the furrow. "No ploughman ever ploughed a straight furrow looking back over his shoulder" (citing Barclay). In following Jesus, we keep our eyes fixed on Him and never look back.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-9/

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### On v. 45 — Why the Meaning Was "Veiled"

- **Reformed (Calvin, Carson):** Emphasise divine sovereignty. The concealment was an intentional act of God — "truth can be plainly spoken yet spiritually inaccessible apart from God's gracious unveiling" (BibleHub). Carson links it to the disciples' own self-absorption (v. 46). Calvin's theology of God's hidden and revealed will underlies this reading.
- **Methodist/Arminian (Clarke):** Clarke (from his commentary) would stress the disciples' own failure rather than a divine decree of concealment — though this specific distinction was not explicit in the material I could access for these verses.
- **Charismatic/Pentecostal (Guzik):** Emphasises the spiritual warfare dimension — the disciples were distracted by ambition (v. 46) and lacked spiritual perception, but focuses less on the theological mechanism of concealment than on the practical lesson.

### On vv. 54–55 — Calling Down Fire

- **Reformed (Calvin, Carson):** Jesus came not to destroy but to save. The disciples' impulse represents a misunderstanding of the present age of grace versus the coming judgment. Carson frames it in terms of Jesus heading to His own death while refusing to kill His enemies.
- **Restoration Movement (Coffman):** Stresses human free will — "God has honoured the freedom of the human will which He created; and all who ever lived are absolutely free to choose either good or evil, only with this limitation, that their choices determine their destiny." God does not retaliate.
- **Dispensational (Constable):** Notes that the Samaritans' rejection was ethnic and religious (temple controversy), not a rejection of Jesus' messianic claim as such. The disciples' proposal reflects an Elijah-model of ministry that Jesus corrects.

### On vv. 57–62 — Radical Discipleship

- **Lutheran:** I was unable to access lcms.org or 1517.org results for these verses in the searches performed.
- **Baptist (Gill):** Gill's approach characteristically focuses on the plain grammatical sense and historical context, without the elaborate theological superstructure.
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** Emphasises the cost of following Jesus as including the renunciation of all earthly security, but reads the passage through the lens of the believer's wholehearted commitment and the urgency of the kingdom mission.

### Textual Note on vv. 55–56

- Several sources (Coffman, Constable) note that some ancient manuscripts include the additional words: "Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man came not to destroy men's lives, but to save them." These words appear in the margin of the ERV (1885) and are considered by many commentators to be authentically Dominical even if not original to Luke's autograph.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/9-53.html
